title: Tippy tap hand-washing station
summary: A hands-free hand-washing station made from a plastic jug, two forked poles, string and a foot pedal, set beside the toilet or kitchen door. You never touch a tap, so clean hands stay clean, and a rock-filled pit underneath stops mud. Soap is the sure choice; ash is an unproven stand-in, and in a Canadian winter the water and the ground freeze.

materials.item: Clean plastic jug or jerry can with a handle and screw cap, 3–5 L
Poles with a forked (Y-shaped) top, about 2 m long
Straight sticks about 1 m long: one crossbar, one foot pedal
Cord or rope: about 1 m for the pedal, 0.5 m for the soap
Nail 8–11 cm long, with pliers or a cloth to hold it
Candle or lighter to heat the nail
Bar of soap and a short piece of stick
Rocks or coarse gravel for the soak pit
Towel or paper to dry hands, with a bin for used paper

steps.text: Choose a spot right beside the toilet or the kitchen door, where people pass every time (HIP card). Keep it on ground that drains, away from the well.
Mark a hole on the jug about 12 cm below the cap, on the side opposite the handle (HIP card, CDC tippy tap).
Heat the nail's point in a flame and press it through the mark. Heat it again and make a second hole in the top of the cap (CDC tippy tap, HIP card).
steps.warn: The nail gets hot enough to burn. Hold it with pliers or a thick cloth, never your fingers.

steps.text: Push the 1 m cord through the cap from the outside, tie a knot inside too big to pull back through, and screw the cap on (HIP card).
Dig two holes about 50 cm deep and 70 cm apart, stand the forked poles in them, and pack the soil hard around them (HIP card).
Slide the crossbar through the jug's handle and rest its ends in the forks, so the jug hangs between the poles (HIP card).
Tie the cord's free end to one end of the pedal stick (CDC tippy tap). Adjust it so one end of the stick rests on the ground and the other hangs about 15 cm up (HIP card).
Make a hole through the soap, thread the 0.5 m cord through, tie it to a short stick, and hang the soap from the crossbar beside the jug (HIP card, CDC tippy tap).
Dig a pit about 40 × 40 cm and 20 cm deep where the water falls, and fill it with rocks so it doesn't turn to mud and breed mosquitoes (HIP card).
Fill the jug with treated water up to the hole (CDC tippy tap, HIP card).
To wash: step on the pedal to tip the jug, wet your hands, let go, soap up and scrub all over, then step on it again to rinse (HIP card). Dry your hands fully (CDC hand FAQ).
Keep it full, wash the jug inside and out every week, replace the soap when it's gone, and replace the sticks before they rot (HIP card).
In frost, bring the jug in at night and top it up with warm water in the morning. Insulate it, and keep a towel or paper by it (WEDC Guide 29).
steps.warn: Hot water scalds: use water you can comfortably hold your hand in, not boiling. Wet hands in the cold chill fast, so dry them completely before going back outside.

notes:
## Why it's worth building

In community trials in low- and middle-income countries, promoting hand-washing cut children's bouts of diarrhoea by about 30 % (rate ratio 0.71, moderate-certainty evidence). In day-care centres and schools in rich countries the drop was similar (0.70, high certainty) (Cochrane hand-washing). A tippy tap makes washing easy right where it matters, and with a foot pedal clean hands never touch a dirty tap.

The washing method (wet, lather, scrub at least 20 seconds, rinse, dry) is in [Handwashing](#ref/reference_sanitation/handwashing).

## Soap first

- Plain soap is enough. Bar and liquid soap both work well, and antibacterial soap has shown no added benefit outside health care (CDC hand FAQ).
- Hanging the bar on a cord keeps it off the ground.
- No soap left? You can make soft soap from wood-ash lye, which burns skin and eyes (goggles and gloves): see [Lye from wood ash](#ref/reference_chemicals/lye_from_wood_ash).

## Ash: what is and isn't known

People with no soap often use ash, and some hygiene cards suggest it, including the one this design comes from (HIP card). The evidence behind it is thin:

- A 2020 Cochrane rapid review found 14 studies of ash for hand cleaning, only one of them randomised (Cochrane ash review).
- In one study, children's hospital visits for diarrhoea were about the same in households using ash and soap, but the certainty of that finding is very low (Cochrane ash review).
- Four studies counted bacteria on hands, but all were at high risk of bias, and the review did not combine them because the methods differed and the results were unclearly reported. The reviewers couldn't tell whether ash works as well as soap, or better than water, mud or nothing at all (Cochrane ash review, Cochrane news).
- Nobody knows whether it harms skin: no study reported on it, though chemicals in ash could damage skin (Cochrane ash review, Cochrane news).

If you do use ash: only cold ash from clean, untreated wood (never ash from trash, painted wood or coal: see [Lye from wood ash](#ref/reference_chemicals/lye_from_wood_ash)), kept dry in a small lidded tin. Rinse it off well, keep it out of eyes, and stop if skin cracks or stings. Wet ash is alkaline (pH up to about 12) and has burned a toddler's skin (Missouri Poison Center): see [Lime, wet cement and lye](#browse/hazards/caustic) for first aid.

Alcohol sanitiser is a backup when there's no water, not a replacement for soap on dirty hands: see [Handwashing](#ref/reference_sanitation/handwashing).

## The water

- Fill it with treated water (CDC tippy tap). Where clean water is short, use the cleanest you have (CDC hand FAQ).
- Warm and cold water remove the same germs (CDC hand FAQ).
- Wash the jug inside and out every week (HIP card).
- Label the jug "WASH WATER, NOT FOR DRINKING".

## Where the water goes

The 40 × 40 cm rock pit under the jug lets rinse water soak away instead of making a mud hole where mosquitoes breed (HIP card). Rinse water from hands is greywater: keep it away from wells and food (see [Greywater](#ref/reference_sanitation/greywater)).

For more water, such as a wash basin, let it settle first (raw wastewater clogs a soak pit) and build a proper soak pit: 1.5 to 4 m deep, never less than 2 m above the groundwater, ideally more than 30 m from any drinking-water source. Dig it with the same care as a latrine pit: see [the VIP latrine](#guides/build_vip_latrine). It doesn't work in clay, hard-packed or rocky ground, or where the ground floods or the water table is high (Compendium).

## In winter

- When the water is very cold, people stop washing, children most of all. Insulate the water container and top it up now and then with warm water. WEDC says hot; keep it to what you can comfortably touch, because hot water scalds and the jug hangs over your hands. Give people something to dry their hands on, because wet hands feel colder as they dry; paper is the most hygienic if there's a bin for it (WEDC Guide 29).
- Frozen ground barely lets water soak away (WEDC Guide 29). Ice builds up under an outdoor tap, so catch the rinse water in a basin and empty it away from paths and the well.
- Don't leave a full jug outside overnight in frost. Indoors, hang the same jug from a hook over a basin or bucket beside a [bucket toilet](#guides/skill_toilets_in_winter).
- When the ground is frozen, hang it from a porch beam or a lashed frame instead of digging posts in.
- See [Cold](#browse/hazards/cold) for frostbite and wet hands.

## Other ways to build it

The CDC version uses no posts: hang the jug by its handle, high enough that the cap cord holds one end of the pedal stick off the ground, so stepping on the stick tips the jug (CDC tippy tap). Any jug with a handle and a screw cap will do.

Put one by every toilet: see [the VIP latrine](#guides/build_vip_latrine) and [the compost toilet](#guides/build_compost_toilet).
